newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia retail weakness sees rate cut talk.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia retail weakness sees rate cut talk.

text.p: Australia's consumers were still not spending in late 1996 despite interest rate cuts, and economists said if they have remained reluctant over the key Christmas period then a fourth rate cut may not be out of the question.

Retail trade rose 0.7 percent in November after a 1.2 percent rise in October. However, the series has not yet recovered all of September's 3.7 percent fall and has been negative in trend terms for the last three months.
The softness was despite the fact that by end-November official interest rates had been lowered twice since July.
"This is an unambigously soft number and confirms the anecdotal evidence that retailers were having great difficulty pre-Christmas," Societe Generale economist Glenn Maguuire said.

Last week, department store group David Jones Ltd said "continuing depressed trading conditions in the key Christmas trading months of November and December" had led it to lower its earnings forecast for the half year to January 25 by up to 50 percent.
The Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) had cut rates twice by the end of November, and cut them again in December.
All up official interest rates have fallen by 150 basis points to 6.00 percent since the first cut on July 31 last year, but at this stage it does not appear to have sparked demand.
"From a monetary policy perspective, they (the data) certainly wouldn't stand in the way of another easing," Commonwealth Bank economist Tim Moloney said.
The trend series has declined for the past four months, something which Citibank chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said had not happened since at least 1961 when the series began.

Over the first 11 months of 1996, retail trade has only risen by 1.0 percent, but some economists said the impact of the November statistics was somewhat lessened by the fact that they preceded the last interest rate reduction on December 11.

"Look at the month it relates to -- it's November," HSBC Group economist Anthony Thompson said. In that sense, the data supported the RBA's decision to cut interest rates in December, but did not add to the case for another rate cut, he said.
However any indication of softness in the key December and January months, which is the peak retailing season, would see the calls for a fourth rate cut grow.

"Any evidence that retail sales were on the weak side over the Christmas/New Year period will re-focus financial market attention on the possibility of a fourth easing in monetary policy," Axiom Funds Management economist Matthew Drennan said.

Economists also said the apparent lack of any significant increase in spending despite the two interest rates cuts by November may reflect the delays in the passing on of lower mortgage rates to consumers.
"Maybe consumers need to see the benefit in their hip pocket from lower mortgage charges before they start spending again," Citibank's Koukoulas said. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
